group.title: More rare verbs
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To formally and publicly give up a belief or claim.
examples: He {abjured} his old political views.
wrong: She abjured the faith and practiced it more proudly than ever.

words.meaning: To give a rough outline of something, or hint at what is to come.
examples: The report {adumbrates} the reforms planned for next year.
wrong: He adumbrated the plan by explaining every small detail in full.

words.meaning: To make someone or something seem greater or more powerful.
examples: The ruler built statues to {aggrandize} himself.
wrong: He aggrandized his role by saying he had done almost nothing.

words.meaning: To make a fear or worry smaller or calmer.
examples: The doctor’s words {allayed} her fears.
wrong: The news allayed his fears, so he became terrified.

words.meaning: To tell someone about something they should know.
examples: Please {apprise} me of any changes to the plan.
wrong: She apprised the team by keeping all the news secret.

words.meaning: To take a power or right without any right to it.
examples: The general {arrogated} the powers of the president.
wrong: She arrogated the role after she was fairly elected to it.

words.meaning: To state something firmly as true.
examples: The witness {averred} that she had seen the man.
wrong: He averred the claim by saying he was not sure at all.

words.meaning: To criticize someone angrily and at length.
examples: The coach {berated} the players after the defeat.
wrong: She berated him with warm praise and a hug.

words.meaning: To grow or develop quickly.
examples: The town’s tech industry has {burgeoned} in recent years.
wrong: The business burgeoned, and it shrank to half its size.

words.meaning: To protest or complain strongly to someone.
examples: Residents {remonstrated} with the council about the noise.
wrong: She remonstrated with the waiter by thanking him for the perfect meal.

words.meaning: To stop resisting and give in.
examples: After weeks of strikes, the company {capitulated} to the demands.
wrong: The army capitulated and fought on bravely for years.

words.meaning: To delay a decision in order to gain time.
examples: The minister {temporized} until the scandal faded.
wrong: He temporized by deciding at once.

words.meaning: To mix two different ideas together as if they were one.
examples: Many people {conflate} wealth with happiness.
wrong: He conflated the two ideas by keeping them carefully apart.

words.meaning: To do something while showing that you think it is beneath you.
examples: The star barely {deigned} to look at the fans.
wrong: She deigned to help, eagerly and without any pride.

words.meaning: To show that you disagree or don’t want to do something.
examples: When asked to speak, she {demurred}, saying she was unprepared.
wrong: He demurred and accepted the offer with great enthusiasm.

words.meaning: To show someone that what they believe is wrong.
examples: Let me {disabuse} you of the idea that this job is easy.
wrong: The facts disabused him of his mistake, so he believed it even more.

words.meaning: To hide your real feelings or plans.
examples: He {dissembled} so well that nobody suspected him.
wrong: She dissembled by telling everyone exactly what she felt.

words.meaning: To remove or rub out something so it can no longer be seen.
examples: Time had {effaced} the names on the gravestones.
wrong: The rain effaced the writing, making it clearer than before.

words.meaning: To involve someone deeply in a conflict or difficult situation.
examples: The company became {embroiled} in a long legal dispute.
wrong: He was embroiled in the scandal, so he had no link to it at all.

words.meaning: To make someone feel weak and tired.
examples: The heat {enervated} the hikers.
wrong: The long sleep enervated her, so she felt full of energy.

words.meaning: To criticize someone or something very severely.
examples: Critics {excoriated} the film for its weak plot.
wrong: The review excoriated the book with nothing but praise.

words.meaning: To make up for a wrong you have done.
examples: He gave money to charity to {expiate} his guilt.
wrong: She expiated her crime by committing another one.

words.meaning: To destroy something completely, down to its roots.
examples: The new law aimed to {extirpate} corruption.
wrong: They extirpated the weeds, so the garden was full of them.

words.meaning: To stir up trouble or violence.
examples: Agents were accused of {fomenting} unrest in the region.
wrong: He fomented the riot by calming the crowd and sending them home.

words.meaning: To deny or argue against something.
examples: No one could {gainsay} the strength of her argument.
wrong: Nobody gainsaid the claim; they all argued against it fiercely.

words.meaning: To persuade someone by clever tricks or flattery.
examples: He {inveigled} his way into the private party.
wrong: She inveigled him into it by asking plainly and honestly.

words.meaning: To make someone used to something unpleasant.
examples: Years in the city had {inured} him to the noise.
wrong: Being inured to cold, she shivered at the first cool breeze.

words.meaning: To criticize someone harshly.
examples: The minister was {lambasted} for her comments.
wrong: The critics lambasted the show by calling it brilliant.

words.meaning: To say unfair and harmful things about someone.
examples: The reporter was accused of {maligning} an innocent man.
wrong: He maligned his rival by praising her honesty.

words.meaning: To be a strong reason against something happening.
examples: The high cost {militates} against building a new stadium.
wrong: The bad weather militated against the trip, so it was perfect for traveling.

words.meaning: To make something less severe without curing it.
examples: The drugs can {palliate} the pain but not cure the illness.
wrong: The medicine palliated the pain, making it much worse.

words.meaning: To avoid giving a direct or honest answer.
examples: When asked about the money, he {prevaricated}.
wrong: She prevaricated by giving a clear and direct answer.

words.meaning: To say publicly that you no longer hold a belief or statement.
examples: The witness {recanted} her earlier testimony.
wrong: He recanted his view by repeating it more strongly.

words.meaning: To officially cancel a decision, or put a stop to something.
examples: The court {quashed} his conviction.
wrong: The judge quashed the ruling and made it stronger.

words.meaning: To make someone feel dull or make an activity useless.
examples: Endless paperwork can {stultify} creative staff.
wrong: The fresh challenges stultified her and made her feel inspired.

words.meaning: To say false and damaging things about someone.
examples: His enemies {traduced} his character in the press.
wrong: She traduced her friend by defending her honor.

words.meaning: To scold someone sharply.
examples: The teacher {upbraided} him for being late again.
wrong: He upbraided her by thanking her warmly.

words.meaning: To spoil or weaken something, or make it invalid.
examples: One mistake {vitiated} the whole experiment.
wrong: The error vitiated the results, making them more reliable.

words.meaning: To get something by gentle, flattering persuasion.
examples: The boy {wheedled} an extra cookie out of his grandmother.
wrong: She wheedled the money from him by demanding it rudely.

words.meaning: To reduce a large group by removing the less useful ones.
examples: We {winnowed} the list of applicants down to five.
wrong: They winnowed the list by adding a hundred more names.
